If History Repeats, Small Caps Will Win in a Landslide
 
Plus, Halloween came early for tech giants
 

Google parent Alphabet lost half a trillion dollars in market value Thursday, weighing more broadly on stocks. Today it’s Amazon and Intel’s turn to drag futures on tech-heavy indexes lower. Just meeting expectations, as Amazon did, isn’t enough when stocks are priced for near-perfection. The premarket pain is spreading to other tech companies, and in particular those closely tied to the data center building boom such as CoreWeave.

No misses since 1946

 

What happens when you combine three sweet ingredients?

 

In the stock market at least, there have been some delicious outcomes. The next six months could be the equivalent of s’mores for investors in smaller U.S. companies.

 

Between the November of a midterm election year and the following April, small-capitalization stocks have had an almost unbelievable average total return of 42% annualized over the past century, according to data from Leuthold Group. By contrast, they’ve lost 4% annualized during the preceding six months.

 

That seems to stem from the combination of three winning patterns—the “best six months” plus midterms plus the “size effect.” Their combined benefit isn’t only strong but also remarkably consistent. One has to go back 80 years to find a midterm year when small caps failed to gain.

 

The relief that investors feel once midterm elections results are known has held steady no matter the political outcome. The main thing seems to be that the uncertainty is over.

 

American elections just happen to be in November, but the stock market’s six-month pattern seems to reinforce it in other markets too. It’s believed to have its origins in the seasonality of money demand when the world economy was dominated by agriculture—planting during spring and harvest in the autumn.

 

The advice to “sell in May and go away” isn’t as reliable as it once was, but it seems to hold up in this particular case. Why is this effect so strong for smaller companies, though?

 

One is that they’re more impacted by market liquidity. When it ebbs during the summer or periods of greater investor caution, small stocks tend to get hit harder. The flip side is that they more than make up for it when investors put fresh money to work. The January effect, for example, tends to be strongest for small caps.

 

The stars have been megacap tech stocks in recent years, but small caps have a superior historical track record overall. Depending on which index one consults, a dollar invested in U.S. small-cap stocks a century ago grew to five or six times as much as one invested in the large-cap S&P 500.

 

There’ll be lots of champagne on ice around the U.S. for victory parties or drowning of sorrows Tuesday night. Investors might have something to celebrate regardless of the outcome.
